newsitem.title: UK: Protestants press Major on N.Irish peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: Protestants press Major on N.Irish peace hopes.

text.p: Northern Irish Protestant leaders due to meet Prime Minister John Major on Wednesday said they wanted reassurances from Britain that it was not doing secret deals with their rivals, the IRA.

David Ervine, head of the Progressive Unionist Party (PUP), said Britain must stick to its policy of demanding a credible ceasefire from the Irish Republican Army, as a condition for allowing the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein into peace talks.
The PUP has been permitted to take part in the talks because its guerrilla arm has been observing a two-year truce in their battle to preserve British rule in Northern Ireland.
A press report earlier this week said the IRA had declared an unofficial ceasefire to try to get Sinn Fein into the talks.
"There can be no political concessions for calling a ceasefire," said Ervine, ahead of talks between Major and pro-British "Loyalist" leaders linked to banned guerrilla groups.
Britain and Sinn Fein have both denied any secret contacts, but Ervine said Northern Irish Protestants were not convinced.
"There is undoubtedly megaphone diplomacy going on between the government and the violent nationalist movement," said Ervine in a media interview.
"I don't think that there is any doubt in the minds of the people of Northern Ireland that there have been contacts passing between them."
The talks between Major, the PUP and the Ulster Democratic Party (UDP) will take place in a climate of further uncertainty about the peace process.

The two "Loyalist" parties say the talks chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell could founder within days because of unreasonable demands by mainstream Unionist pro-British parties for early disarmament by the rival guerrilla bands.

UDP leader Gary McMichael said that all parties must try to make common ground and forge ahead. "Republicans must make up their own minds on whether they are prepared to come into the process or not under reasonable terms," he said.
The IRA abandoned a 17-month truce in February setting off bombs in a new phase of a 27-year battle against British rule.

British and Irish ministers spearheading a bid to end IRA violence and bring Sinn Fein into the talks were to meet in Belfast late on Wednesday to assess strategy in the light of mixed signals from the republicans.

Police foiled a suspected IRA attack on security forces in Londonderry last weekend. It would have been the first IRA attack in the province since car bombs killed a soldier and wounded 30 at Britain's army headquarters south of Belfast on October 7.
